Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 80, verse 18–32:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ ﴿From a drop of seminal fluid He created him and determined him.﴾ ﴿Then He made the way easy for him.﴾ ﴿Then He causes him to die and buries him.﴾ ﴿Then, when He wills, He will raise him again.﴾ ﴿No! He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him.﴾ ﴿So let man look at his food:﴾ ﴿that We pour down the water abundantly,﴾ ﴿then We split the earth asunder,﴾ ﴿and cause grain to grow therein,﴾ ﴿and grapes and herbage,﴾ ﴿and olives and palm trees,﴾ ﴿and gardens dense with trees,﴾ ﴿and fruit and pasture,﴾ ﴿as a provision for you and your cattle.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ is an interrogative intended as an affirmation of the insignificance of the thing from which He created man. It is an expression that may serve either belittlement or exaltation, and the context clarifies the purpose. This is similar to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For what day were they postponed?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 12] ﴿For the Day of Decision﴾ [al-Mursalat: 13]. The "nutfah" (drop) referred to is the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman. Most readers read "faqaddarahu" with a doubled dal, and some readers read "faqdarahu" with it lightened. The meaning is: He made him with a single known measure of limbs, form, lifespan and other things, from his begetting, according to His will, in each individual person.

The interpreters differed over the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then He made the way easy for him.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Abu Salih and al-Suddi said: it is the way of exit from the womb of the woman. Al-Hasan said, in substance: the way is the way of upright reflection which leads to faith, and its being made easy for him is the bestowal of intellect. Mujahid said: He intended the way in general, the noun of genus as in "guidance and misguidance," meaning: He made it easy for some people for this and for other people for that, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, either grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 3].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then He causes him to die and buries him﴾ means: He commanded that a grave be made for him, and in that is honour, so that he is not cast away like the rest of the animals. The "qabir" is the one who undertakes placing the dead in his grave, and the "muqbir" is the one who orders the burial of the dead and arranges it. "Anshara" means: He gave him life; it is said: "nashara al-mayyit" and "anshara-hu Allah" (God raised the dead). His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿when He wills﴾ means: when the time He has willed for it arrives, and that is the Day of Resurrection. Some readers read "idha sha'a anshara-hu" with both hamzas pronounced clearly; most readers read "idha sha'a anshara-hu" with a long vowel and softening of the first hamza; Shu'ayb ibn Abi Hamzah read "idha sha'a nashara-hu"; and al-A'mash read "idha anshara-hu" with a single hamza.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿No! He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ is a rejection of whatever objections the unbelievers might raise against these narrated statements, and a emphatic negation of man's obedience to his Lord, and an affirmation that he has neglected the right of God, may He be exalted, and has not fulfilled what He commanded him. Mujahid said: No one ever fulfils what is obligatory upon him. Then God, may He be exalted, commanded man to take lesson and to look at his food and the evidence in it. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and others held that what is meant by "to his food" is his food once it has become waste, so that he may reflect on where the outcome of this world leads, and upon what its people perish and on what its millstone turns. This is similar to what is related from Ibn 'Umar, that when a man defecates, an angel takes hold of his forelock at the end, turns his gaze toward it, making him stand and reflect, and this benefits whoever has intellect. The majority held that the meaning of the verse is: let him look at what he eats, and how God makes it provided for him through these intermediaries mentioned, namely the pouring of water and the splitting of the earth. It is related that a worshipper hosted a man, and he set before him a dry, bare loaf; the man seemed to find it coarse, so he said to him: "Eat it, for God has not bestowed it and perfected it until three hundred and sixty workers were subjected to it: water, wind and sun, these three being among them."
